audience: Senior engineers and software delivery leaders, with research context.
positioning: Practical lessons from SDLCAI about how AI changes software delivery, review, understanding and discovery. Use named examples, preserve trade-offs, and give readers something to examine in their own team.
linkedinApproach: Lead with one engineering question or concrete example. Add a useful qualification and a timestamped source. Use LinkedIn to introduce the discussion and point to the full article or recording.

series.title: Where does the bottleneck move when code gets cheaper?
series.summary: Compare faster implementation with the work of choosing, reviewing, verifying and operating changes. Frame this around delivery outcomes rather than output volume.
series.question: Which part of your delivery flow becomes constrained as implementation speeds up?
series.linkedinAngle: Introduce Mo's bottleneck argument, then connect it to Sini's production journey. Invite readers to describe what actually queues up in their team.
series.qualification: The seminar examples support a comparison of experiences, not a universal productivity estimate.

series.title: Who owns a change proposed by an agent?
series.summary: Explore the boundaries between proposing, planning, testing, approving and deploying. Use concrete incidents and different review models to make the choices visible.
series.question: What can an agent change, and what evidence does a person need before approving it?
series.linkedinAngle: Start with Viljami's deployment near miss. Pair the incident with Ohans's earlier plan review and link to the full explanations.
series.qualification: The speakers describe different operating models. A second model does not by itself establish independent verification.

series.title: Keeping engineering understanding current
series.summary: Connect system understanding, decision rationale and shared context with the cost of maintaining that knowledge. Examine ownership and relevance rather than simply producing more documentation.
series.question: How do people and agents learn why the system works this way, and who keeps that explanation useful?
series.linkedinAngle: Pair Waseem's argument about knowledge outside the code with the final Q&A's concern about decision-record overhead.
series.qualification: Keep the final Q&A quote attributed to the session unless the individual speaker is confirmed. Selected editorial wording is not a verified verbatim quotation.

series.title: What do we learn by building?
series.summary: Bring the research sessions into a practical discussion of probes, generated interfaces and repeatable experiments. Show how building can change the problem a team is trying to solve.
series.question: When is a prototype helping you discover the problem, and how will you evaluate what it teaches you?
series.linkedinAngle: Introduce Tapio's probe, then retain Joongi's Q&A qualification that building and testing can change the problem itself.
series.qualification: Preserve the differences between product discovery, interface research and scientific experimentation. Zak's medical examples describe research rather than established clinical outcomes.

posters.title: Minimum Viable Disclosure
posters.summary: Data minimisation, recommendation quality and re-identification risk, including the effect of popularity bias.

posters.title: Hypermedia as a Substrate for the Agentic Web
posters.summary: Exposing state-dependent actions through hypermedia, with a shared model for human and agent interfaces.

posters.title: Software Engineering in Safety and Mission Critical Applications
posters.summary: AI-assisted engineering for safety and mission critical systems, with examples from Aalto University's industrial automation research.
